analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to all wages and raises retiree benefits.
analysis.headline: A Social Security expansion with 66 Democratic cosponsors never received a committee hearing or floor vote in the 113th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lifted the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes, phasing it out so that by 2018 every dollar of earnings, not just earnings up to roughly the current cap, would be taxed [S3]. It would use some of that revenue to raise benefits: adding earnings above the old cap into the benefit formula, increasing the benefit formula itself by up to 15 percent over time, and switching to a retiree-specific inflation index that would produce larger annual cost-of-living increases [S2] [S3]. It was referred to two committees and never taken up [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, including current retirees and future retirees, would get higher monthly checks and larger annual cost-of-living adjustments, with increases growing to 15 percent in the benefit formula for people becoming eligible after 2018 [S3]. The program's finances would also improve, since taxing earnings above the cap brings in substantial revenue [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill phases in taxation of all wages above the current contribution and benefit base: 80 percent of wages above the cap would be taxed starting in 2014, with the taxable share rising until all such wages are taxed from 2018 onward [S3].

Retirees would see larger checks: 5 percent of earnings above the old cap would count toward benefits, and the benefit formula's bend points would increase by 1 percentage point a year starting in 2019, reaching 15 percent by 2033 [S3].

Cost-of-living increases would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish to track the spending patterns of people at retirement age, a basket that typically rises faster than the index currently used [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and self-employed high earners would pay the 12.4 percent combined Social Security payroll tax on every dollar of earnings instead of only on earnings up to the annual cap, a change phased in from 2014 through 2017 [S3]. Employers would pay the matching share of that tax on high-wage payrolls [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill is a substantial tax increase on affluent households and self-employed professionals, who would pay the full payroll tax on all earnings from 2018 onward with only a small additional benefit credit of 5 percent of above-cap earnings, meaning most of the new revenue would not come back to them as benefits [S3].

Switching the cost-of-living index to one based on retirees' spending would make benefits grow faster and add to the program's long-term cost, which is part of why the bill requires new appropriations for the Bureau of Labor Statistics to build and publish the index [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad: higher checks and faster cost-of-living increases for tens of millions of beneficiaries, plus revenue that improves the program's finances [S2] [S3]. The cost is real but concentrated: it falls almost entirely on high earners and employers of high-wage workers through the payroll tax [S3]. On the merits, the trade is one where a diffuse public gain is paid for by a narrow group, which is also why it faced a wall in a committee controlled by the other party.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee, first at Ways and Means and then at an Education and Workforce subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2013 by Rep. Linda T. Sánchez and referred to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee [S1] [S5].
It drew 66 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
In January 2014 it was referred to the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee, which is a further delay rather than progress toward a vote, and no further action followed [S5].
No vote of any kind was ever taken on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and employers of high-wage workers are better off because the bill died, since they would have paid Social Security payroll tax on all earnings. Beneficiaries lost the higher checks and faster cost-of-living increases the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who kept the payroll tax cap

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 66 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp

against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.what_they_did: Chaired the second committee of referral; the bill was parked at a subcommittee and never brought up.

sides.party_line_note: All 66 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill never advanced [S4].

industries.note: They would have paid the full 12.4 percent payroll tax on every dollar of earnings starting in 2018 instead of only on wages up to the annual cap [S3]. Their interest in keeping the cap runs directly against beneficiaries' interest in higher, better-indexed benefits.
Employers pay the matching half of Social Security payroll tax, so firms with high-paid workforces would face a new tax on wages above the cap [S3].
Higher benefit formula and a retiree-specific inflation index would mean larger checks both upfront and through faster annual increases [S3].
